On Euronews' first edition of Europe Tonight, presenter Mared Gwyn Jones led a debate on Europe's latest migration crackdown, after five EU countries announced a partnership with Rwanda to establish deportation hubs for irregular migrants.

In the first edition of Euronews' new flagship show, Europe Tonight, presenter Mared Gwyn Jones brought viewers the latest analysis of the stories making headlines over the weekend and on Monday.

Jones opened the programme with the latest EU developments on migration, as five countries - Greece, Denmark, Germany, Austria and the Netherlands - announced a partnership with Rwanda to establish deportation hubs for irregular migrants, with the first pilot centres expected to be operational by mid-2027.

Our correspondent Vincenzo Genovese, reporting from Vienna, said it marked an unprecedented move in EU migration policy, with the bloc sending irregular migrants to a country with which they have no previous connection - a move compared to Donald Trump's approach in the US.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called the agreement a "game changer," saying it would help European countries regain control and remove incentives for illegal migrants.

According to people familiar with the negotiations, the first facility will accommodate around 100 people. The hub would consist of open facilities rather than closed deportation centres, and migrants would be free to move around the country. The goal is to give them the chance to integrate into local society and the labour market.

The EU law enabling return hubs outside the bloc states that only non-EU countries “where international human rights standards are respected” are eligible.

Rwanda has a questionable track record on human rights. However, Rwanda's minister of the interior, Vincent Biruta, said the country was ready, had good experience in dealing with migrants and would respect fundamental rights.

Legal challenges could emerge when deportations begin next year, as happened with the UK-Rwanda agreement.

On Monday, Frederiksen added that she had a strong feeling that other countries would join the scheme.

Nineteen of the twenty-seven EU governments support the deportation plan. Only France and Spain have made clear their opposition to it. Italy already has its own agreement with Albania.

THE DEBATE

MEPs Charlie Weimers and Abir Al-Sahlani discuss Rwanda

Jones hosted Swedish MEP Charlie Weimers, a Member of the European Parliament since 2019 and part of the European Conservatives and Reformists group, and Iraqi-born Swedish MEP Abir Al-Sahlani of the Renew Europe Group, who has also been an MEP since 2019, to debate the Rwanda "Return Hub."

Weimers said he agreed with Frederiksen, adding that he thought the policy was a "game changer." Noting that "every system" starts small, he said it would be successful if it led to further steps in the future to address migration policy in the EU.

Al-Sahlani pondered the feasibility of Rwanda returning migrants to their countries of origin, questioning how Rwanda would be able to carry out such returns when European countries themselves had struggled to do so.

“If we in Europe were not able to send them back to their countries, what makes us believe Rwanda will be able to?” Al-Sahlani asked, citing concerns over Rwanda's dependence on development aid and security concerns, as well as other unanswered questions.

Weimers calls deal a 'deterrent'

Meanwhile, Jones challenged Weimers over the cost-effectiveness of the proposed centres, citing Italy’s Albania scheme, which is costing Italian taxpayers €670 million over five years while handling only 0.3% of illegal arrivals into Italy. But Weimers described the new deal as being intended as a "deterrent" to those considering illegally migrating to Europe.

Al-Sahlani also criticised the growing influence of far-right narratives on European migration policy, arguing that governments were failing to use existing legislation and tools effectively.

The Renew Europe Group MEP further accused political leaders of portraying refugees as a threat and making them scapegoats for wider societal problems. She also warned that migration debates were increasingly driven by emotion rather than facts, fuelled by the misuse of statistics, selective truths and fabricated stories that vilify people seeking refuge.

Under new rules, public bodies such as municipalities and towns are to be generally liable for VAT when they engage in commercial activities.

Controversy is brewing in Germany over the country's so-called "bratwurst tax."

From 1 January, new VAT rules are set to apply across all German municipalities, potentially meaning that key local community groups such as volunteer fire brigades could have to pay tax on sales of things such as bratwursts at village festivals and other local events.

The changes stem from section 2b of Germany's VAT Act, which has been repeatedly delayed but which is now expected to come into force. Under the rules, public bodies such as municipalities and towns are to be generally liable for VAT when they engage in commercial activities.

That means if a volunteer fire brigade operates as part of the municipality and not as an independent association, VAT would have to be paid on sales at local events.

Since 1 January 2026, a reduced tax rate of 7% has applied to food sold at snack bars or in restaurants. However, those affected have to keep detailed records of their sales and issue receipts.

On the website "Kommunal.de," Christian Erhardt-Maciejewski has taken a satirical swipe at the tax in a piece titled "Hurrah, the tax office is grilling the fire brigade."

He writes: "I can already imagine what will happen now: the most resourceful brigades will set up a support association so that they can carry on selling sausages. The fire brigade festival becomes an association festival, the grill master turns into a treasurer, mustard becomes a question for the statutes. A whole new form of volunteering is born in Germany: finding ways to dodge the tax authorities."

In the Schleswig-Holstein state parliament, the CDU, Greens and FDP are calling for the new rules to be put on hold or for additional exemptions to be introduced.

"If the bratwurst at the Easter bonfire becomes a case for the tax office, something has gone seriously wrong," Christopher Vogt, the chair of the FDP parliamentary group, said, per NDR.

Vogt urged the state government in Kiel to "urgently provide support for local volunteers."

There has already been some movement in North Rhine-Westphalia, where the state's finance minister, Marcus Optendrenk, reportedly issued a decree clarifying that bratwurst sales by volunteer fire brigades are to be exempt from VAT.

"Anyone who volunteers with the local fire brigade deserves a tailwind rather than paperwork," Optendrenk said.

Țușpaisul este o garnitură de legume, servită alături de ouă, de cartofi noi fripți, de pui fript sau de chiftele. Legumele se schimbă după anotimp. Vara se face din ludăiță (dovlecel) sau din călărabă (gulie), primăvara devreme din spanac și mazăre, iar iarna din morcovi.

Astăzi este o echipă foarte mică, de aproximativ 10 oameni, dintre care unii contribuie cu jumătate de normă, în timp ce lucrează și la alte proiecte.

Cel mai tânăr membru al echipei, inginerul nostru de comunicații, are 25 de ani. Părinții lui nici nu se născuseră când a fost lansată Voyager. Alți membri ai echipei lucrau deja la misiune când aceasta a fost lansată. Unii s-au pensionat, dar s-au întors ca să ne ofere o parte din timpul lor și să contribuie cu ce știu despre misiune.

Cel mai în vârstă dintre noi, expert în computerul sistemului de date de zbor, tocmai a împlinit 90 de ani.

Care este misiunea sondei Voyager 2?

Fiecare dintre sondele Voyager se îndreaptă în direcții ușor diferite. 

Voyager 1 se deplasează spre nord față de planul planetelor, după ce a vizitat Jupiter, Saturn și Titan, satelitul lui Saturn. 

Voyager 2 se îndreaptă spre sud, după ce a vizitat Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus și Neptun. Cele două sonde colectează date din zone diferite ale spațiului interstelar, iar noi putem compara aceste măsurători pentru a căuta asemănările și deosebirile dintre ele. 

Voyager 2 se deplasează ceva mai încet, așa că nu va depăși distanța de o zi-lumină decât în 2035. Până atunci, nu va mai avea suficientă energie pentru a trimite semnale înapoi spre Pământ.

Ce date trimite sonda spațială astăzi?

Voyager 1 explorează spațiul interstelar cu antena îndreptată permanent spre Pământ, pentru a putea comunica. Asta înseamnă că sonda trimite date tot timpul, doar că depinde de momentul în care avem acoperire prin antenele rețelei Deep Space Network a NASA pentru a recepționa toate datele. 

Sonda și-a început misiunea interplanetară în 1977 cu zece instrumente și un experiment de radioștiință. Când și-a început misiunea interstelară, în 1990, funcționau cinci instrumente. Dar, pentru că Voyager 1 pierde patru wați de putere pe an, a trebuit să oprim treptat diverse sisteme. 

În prezent, mai funcționează doar două instrumente: magnetometrul și subsistemul pentru unde de plasmă.

Ce ne spun aceste instrumente despre spațiul interstelar, pe care Voyager 1 este prima sondă care îl vizitează?

Sonda trimite măsurători continue ale câmpurilor magnetice și ale undelor de plasmă. Aceste date ne aduc din când în când surprize. 

Inițial, ne așteptam ca densitatea plasmei de electroni și intensitatea câmpului magnetic să scadă treptat, pe măsură ce sonda lasă în urmă sistemul nostru solar, dar am descoperit că lucrurile nu stau neapărat așa. 

În 2020, Voyager 1 a înregistrat un eveniment puternic, provenit probabil de la Soare, care a făcut ca atât intensitatea câmpului magnetic, cât și densitatea plasmei de electroni să crească brusc, iar de atunci nu au mai scăzut. 

Aceasta este una dintre marile bucurii ale științei spațiale: obții date pe care nu te-ai fi așteptat să le obții pe baza modelelor și teoriilor actuale, așa că trebuie să le adaptezi și să dezvolți teorii noi.

Voyager 1 a fost proiectată inițial pentru o misiune de patru ani, iar acum a ajuns aproape la 50. Care este secretul longevității sale?

Evoluția tehnologiei a făcut operațiunile mult mai ușoare.

Când am început să lucrez la misiune, în 1977, desenam cronogramele observațiilor pe o coală lungă de hârtie de calc, cu rigla și creionul. Astăzi, putem genera aceste cronograme automat, pe calculator.

După standardele de azi, tehnologia de la bordul sondei pare străveche: Voyager 1 are dimensiunea unei mașini mici. Computerul ei este cât o servietă mică și are mai puțină memorie decât telefonul mobil pe care îl aveți astăzi. Pe de altă parte, această tehnologie veche s-ar putea să fi contribuit la longevitatea sondei.

În ce sens?

În spațiu, echipamentele sunt lovite în permanență de razele cosmice. Dacă ai componente mai mari, este mai puțin probabil ca o singură lovitură a unei raze cosmice să afecteze o parte semnificativă din ele. Dacă ai funcționa cu un singur cip mic, care ar fi avariat de o rază cosmică, ai pierde o cantitate uriașă de informații.

Când telescopul spațial Hubble s-a defectat, NASA a putut trimite astronauți să repare oglinda și să înlocuiască bateriile. Voyager 1 se află la miliarde de kilometri distanță, astfel că nu poți pur și simplu să trimiți un tehnician. Cum depanează echipa dumneavoastră o sondă aflată atât de departe?

Uneori trebuie să improvizăm.

Într-o zi din 2024, Voyager 1 a început să trimită date fără niciun sens. Ne-am dat seama că unul dintre cipuri fusese avariat, probabil de o rază cosmică. A fost nevoie să modificăm programul, astfel încât să ocolească acel cip. Am lucrat luni de zile la secvența de cod și apoi am trimis-o sondei. Cum Voyager 1 se afla la aproape o zi-lumină distanță, a durat aproape două zile ca o comandă de pe Pământ să ajungă la ea și ca răspunsul ei să se întoarcă pe Pământ. Așteptarea a fost chinuitoare... Dar într-o dimineață de aprilie am început din nou să primim date: reparația de la distanță reușise. Am izbucnit cu toții în urale.

Ați fost alături de misiunile Voyager încă de la început. Cum ați ajuns să lucrați la ele?

Am început să lucrez la Jet Propulsion Laboratory al NASA în 1977, imediat după ce mi-am terminat licența în fizică. Când mi s-a oferit ocazia să lucrez la misiunile interplanetare Voyager, am fost încântată: îmi amintesc că, în clasa a treia, aveam un telescop micuț cu care mă uitam la Lună, la sateliții lui Jupiter și la inelele lui Saturn. Abia așteptam să văd aceste lumi mai de aproape.

Am fost responsabilă de coordonarea observațiilor științifice până în 1990, apoi am trecut la misiunea Cassini. În 2020 m-am întors la programul Voyager, iar doi ani mai târziu am preluat conducerea științifică.

Sondele Voyager au dus o călătorie lungă. Care au fost, pentru dumneavoastră, momentele cele mai memorabile ale acestei misiuni?

Am fost acolo și am privit cum racheta care transporta Voyager 2 se ridica de pe rampa de lansare pentru a-și începe călătoria. A fost minunat să fac parte din această călătorie încă de la început. Momentul misiunii a fost, de asemenea, perfect ales: doar o dată la 176 de ani se aliniază planetele astfel încât să poți survola Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus și Neptun dintr-o singură trecere. 

Voyager 2 a fost prima și, până acum, singura navă spațială care a vizitat patru planete în cursul unei singure misiuni. Pentru mine, un alt moment memorabil a fost trecerea pe lângă sateliții lui Jupiter: ei ne-au oferit cele mai mari surprize dintre toate.

De ce?

În ceea ce privește sateliții, nu aveam prea multe repere de comparație, așa că presupuneam că toți arată ca Luna noastră: lumi vechi, acoperite de cratere. Apoi am ajuns la sateliții lui Jupiter. 

Ganymede prezenta semne de deplasare tectonică a scoarței. Europa, de un alb strălucitor și acoperită de gheață, nu are aproape deloc cratere. Și, în sfârșit, Io: pe acest satelit micuț am văzut vulcani activi, care erupeau chiar în timp ce treceam pe lângă el. 

Nimic din toate acestea nu se potrivea cu modelul nostru despre sateliți, așa că am învățat pur și simplu să ne așteptăm la neașteptat.

Cum urmăreați toate acestea la momentul respectiv?

În clădirea în care lucram erau monitoare TV în cantină, în sălile de conferințe și cam peste tot în jur. Aveam o listă cu evenimentele care urmau să aibă loc și cu orele la care se petreceau: o privire de aproape asupra unui anumit satelit al lui Saturn, o fotografie a inelelor lui Uranus care urma să sosească.

Uneori îmi aduceam sacul de dormit, pentru că unele dintre cele mai frumoase lucruri se întâmplau noaptea. Mulți dintre noi dormeam sub birouri și ne puneam ceasul să sune, ațipind până când venea momentul să ne trezim. Iar când imaginile apăreau pe ecrane, oamenii săreau în picioare și arătau spre ele: „Ce crezi că e asta? Îți vine să crezi?” 

A fost minunat să fiu acolo și să trăiesc toate acestea.

Înainte de misiunile Voyager, aveam doar o idee vagă despre planete precum Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus și Neptun. Acum, pentru prima dată, puteam vedea aceste lumi îndepărtate la rezoluție înaltă. Cum au schimbat aceste sonde felul în care ne imaginăm universul?

Programul Voyager a schimbat felul în care privim sistemul nostru solar. Și astăzi, unele dintre fotografiile emblematice realizate de Voyager 1 și Voyager 2 sunt încă folosite în sălile de clasă și în manuale.

Voyager a pus, de asemenea, bazele misiunilor care au urmat: ne-a arătat suprafețele de un alb strălucitor ale sateliților Europa și Enceladus, explorați mai târziu de misiunile Galileo și Cassini ale NASA. Aceste misiuni au descoperit că ambii sateliți sunt acoperiți de o crustă de gheață, sub care se află un ocean de apă lichidă. Asta a dus la noi întrebări: ar putea exista, de fapt, viață în aceste oceane? 

În prezent, misiunea Europa Clipper  este pe drum pentru a explora această posibilitate. Voyager a răspuns la multe întrebări și ne-a adus o mulțime de întrebări noi și captivante.

Longevitatea sondei Voyager 1 este impresionantă, dar sonda nu este nemuritoare. Când va înceta să mai comunice cu Pământul?

Nu știm. Se poate întâmpla astăzi sau peste câțiva ani.

La fel ca în cazul corpului uman, și o sondă spațială dă semne de îmbătrânire odată cu trecerea timpului: conductele de combustibil se înfundă, iar sursa de energie pe bază de plutoniu se degradează treptat. S-ar putea să vină o zi în care nu vom mai primi semnalul de la Voyager 1.

Ca întotdeauna, vom încerca să vedem dacă putem repune nava în funcțiune. Dar dacă nimic nu va funcționa, va trebui pur și simplu să acceptăm că misiunea de explorare a sondei s-a încheiat și că ea va prelua o altă misiune: va deveni un ambasador tăcut al omenirii.

Vă referiți la Discul de Aur pe care îl poartă ambele sonde Voyager, un disc fonografic din cupru placat cu aur, cu mesaje de salut în 55 de limbi, imagini ale Pământului și tot felul de muzică. De ce a trimis NASA așa ceva în spațiu?

Discul a fost conceput ca un mesaj cosmic într-o sticlă, care să le facă cunoscută existența noastră unor eventuale civilizații extraterestre. Pe copertă se află o hartă care arată poziția sistemului nostru solar în galaxie, raportată la pulsarii din apropiere.

Peste aproximativ 40.000 de ani, Voyager 1 va trece relativ aproape de o altă stea. Cine știe, poate cineva de acolo ne va găsi mesajul și va veni să ne viziteze.

Ar fi acesta un vis al dumneavoastră? Să fim vizitați de extratereștri sau să primim un semnal de la ei?

M-am întrebat întotdeauna dacă există viață și în alte părți ale universului. Ar fi un vis devenit realitate să fim vizitați de o formă de viață inteligentă sau să primim un semnal de la ea.

Discul de Aur poate rezista până la un miliard de ani și s-ar putea foarte bine să supraviețuiască omenirii. Ce mesaj ați vrea să ducă Voyager 1 în univers?

Pentru mine, mesajul este simplu: a existat o civilizație care a avut inteligența și tehnologia necesare pentru a construi această navă spațială și pentru a o trimite spre stele. Asta mă umple de un sentiment uriaș de mândrie.

The next FIFA presidential election is due to take place at the 77th FIFA Congress on Thursday, 18 March 2027 in Rabat, Morocco.

French football chief Philippe Diallo is set to run for the FIFA presidency as a surprise late candidate in next year's elections.

European governing body UEFA proposed Diallo on Monday following a meeting of its executive committee.

"Diallo has accepted the invitation to stand. His candidacy is due to be formally ratified by the FFF Executive Committee at its meeting tomorrow," UEFA said in a statement, adding that Diallo had "extensive experience across all levels of the game."

Diallo is lined up to run against Japanese official Kozo Tashima and incumbent President Gianni Infantino, who is seeking to shake off a major crisis that has dominated sporting headlines in recent months.

Infantino, who was first elected as president in 2016, came under huge pressure in the summer after FIFA announced a highly controversial private investment plan that would have seen third-party investors invited to take stakes in a commercial subsidiary dubbed the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE).

The proposal, which was later scrapped, drew fierce pushback from across the football community, with some accusing the world governing body of looking to "sell" the sport.

"Against the backdrop of serious concerns over the direction of FIFA, the national associations called for renewed unity and trust within the global football community," UEFA said on Monday.

"They expressed their full confidence in Philippe Diallo to provide the leadership needed to achieve this ambition," it added.

FIFA confirmed in September that Infantino, who has also faced questions over his relationship with US President Donald Trump, would stand for re-election.

"The FIFA President announced in April that he will stand for re-election in 2027. Of course, nothing has changed. Mr Infantino will be standing for re-election," a spokesperson said.

The presidential election is due to take place at the 77th FIFA Congress on Thursday, 18 March 2027 in Rabat, Morocco.

Serbia’s Student List will speed up rule-of-law reforms needed for EU accession, MP Aleksandar Baucal said in the movement’s first international appearance.

The Student List will speed up work on meeting the EU’s interim accession benchmarks on the rule of law, professor and newly elected MP Aleksandar Baucal said in the much-awaited first international public appearance of Serbia's new main political force.

“The next question is whether Serbia will remain on the European path. For us, the European path is one of reforms: strengthening European values, building functional institutions and a genuine rule-of-law system, developing a sustainable economy integrated in the European market,” Baucal said on Monday.

Baucal spoke at the EU Enlargement Forum in Brussels, the first time a Student List representative has addressed an international audience. Most of the room gave him a standing ovation after the speech.

For the professor, the EU accession path is not only key for good neighbourly relations, but, more broadly, for building a more democratic society.

“One of Serbia’s strategic objectives will be to accelerate the fulfilment of the interim benchmarks under chapters 23 and 24, as well. We want Serbia to be a reliable partner to the European Union and to its members,” he continued.

The party’s historic electoral victory last month raised hopes of a reset in Serbia’s troubled relations with the EU. The movement, born of nearly two years of mass protests, ousted Aleksandar Vučić’s party after 14 years in power.

Two weeks ago, Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos met a Student List delegation in Brussels, their first formal exchange with a senior EU official. The delegates said the incoming government would focus on restoring the rule of law, judicial independence and media freedom, not only for the sake of accession but above all for the Serbian people.

Baucal returned to those themes, pledging to advance on the “fundamentals” of EU accession. The professor-turned-MP said the new government would stay open to dialogue and seek to solve concrete problems rather than create new ones.

“This is not only about the European Union helping Serbia protect democracy. It is also about a democratic Serbia contributing to a stronger and more resilient Europe,” he said.

Yet prominent figures in the Student List remain cautious about aligning with EU foreign policy, notably on sanctions against Russia. These are deeply unpopular in Serbia, where memories of the Western sanctions that hit the population under the Milošević regime still run deep.

Recognition of Kosovo could also prove a sticking point with EU countries. Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama warned that the new government is unlikely to change Serbia’s stance.

The Student List grew as a heterogeneous movement without a clearly defined leadership. Belgrade’s position on accession and foreign policy may become clearer once its MPs settle on the make-up of the new government.

For now, Baucal sees the party’s next challenge as turning the solidarity forged in the struggle into lasting trust in institutions.

“Citizens were able to set many differences aside. But in a democratic society, these interests and opinions will once again come to the fore. We believe that thanks to our differences, we will build a better system for our citizens,” he said.

Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece aim to begin deporting rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda in 2027, despite concerns over human rights and potential legal challenges.

Five EU countries announced a partnership with Rwanda on Monday to establish the first EU return hub outside the bloc, marking a radical hardening of European migration policy.

Although the details of the agreement are still being negotiated, Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece say they are confident of reaching a deal and beginning deportations of irregular migrants in 2027.

The first facility is expected to accommodate around 100 people at a time. Those sent there will be free to move around Rwanda and are expected to integrate into local society and the labour market, according to officials.

“I think this [agreement] is a game changer. We will take back control and remove the incentive for illegal migration,” said Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, during the announcement in Vienna, along with Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker and the interior ministers of other countries involved, including Rwanda’s Vincent Biruta.

The initial hub will be a small-scale pilot project, with plans to expand the scheme once it is operational and the risk of deportations being blocked by legal challenges has diminished.

Who will be sent to the return hubs?

The five countries will deport only rejected asylum seekers who are subject to enforceable return decisions.

Minors will be excluded, while each country will apply its own criteria for selecting those to be deported.

The Netherlands will focus on adult men from countries in Rwanda’s region, while Germany will target migrants who refuse to cooperate with efforts to establish their identity and come from countries reluctant to readmit their own nationals, according to people familiar with the negotiations.

After a period at the facility, the length of which has yet to be determined, migrants will be expected to rebuild their lives in Rwanda or voluntarily return to their countries of origin or another country where they have the right to reside.

The EU border agency Frontex will not have a role in deportations in the initial stages, despite a reform of its mandate recently proposed by the European Commission, which would allow it to do so.

Costs remain unclear

The five EU countries will bear the full cost of deporting migrants and accommodating them in Rwanda. However, no estimate for the initial facility was provided at the press conference, as negotiations are still ongoing.

According to people familiar with the negotiations, services in Rwanda will be considerably cheaper than equivalent services in Europe.

What Rwanda will get in return is also unclear at this stage. Kigali is, however, set to sign a partnership agreement with Denmark next week, related to cooperation on migration.

“The agreement is a shame”

Return hubs have raised concerns over their compatibility with EU law and the protection of human rights.

Critics warn they could lead to human rights violations, particularly when established in countries with limited democratic standards.

“The agreement is a shame,” said French lawmaker Mélissa Camara, of the Greens/EFA group, considering the countries involved are “crossing another disgraceful moral line by reaching an agreement with an authoritarian regime.”

The group of five countries said that all procedures will be carried out in line with international human rights standards.

However, legal complications may arise when deportations to Rwanda begin next year, as the European Court of Human Rights prohibits countries from transferring individuals to states or situations where they may be subjected to violations of fundamental rights.

The United Nations has raised concerns about Rwanda's human rights record.

A similar agreement between Rwanda and the United Kingdom, under which Britain planned to send asylum seekers to the African country, was ruled unlawful by the UK Supreme Court in 2023 because of the risk that those transferred could subsequently be sent to countries where they faced persecution.

According to the law enabling EU states to set up return hubs outside the bloc, only non-EU countries — “where international human rights standards and principles in accordance with international law are respected” — are eligible.

UN Secretary General and Pope Leo XIV have urged countries to agree stricter rules for autonomous weapon systems, to stop them from being given the ability to make life and death decisions without human intervention.

Killer robots and drones are coming up for a reckoning this week as government envoys on Monday revved up a discussion and could decide this week whether to launch negotiations toward setting rules for use of the deadly machines — or not.

Pope Leo XIV, the UN chief and advocacy groups have framed the issue as an existential debate: Whether robots can be allowed to kill and whether humans must maintain some control of and accountability for use of lethal autonomous weapon systems.

Activists say armed drones that can independently strike targets have already been deployed in some select instances in conflict zones like Ukraine and the Middle East, but widespread rollout hasn’t happened.

Scary would-be scenarios, like armed drones flying amok and gunning down civilians with pinpoint precision, have peppered years of discussions about killer robots. But those talks haven't produced any international restrictions.

The United States and Russia, longtime rivals, want to limit any curbs on their ability to develop and deploy powerful new tools in the high-tech arms race — just as AI is gaining steam and changing battle plans.

Proponents of an AI weaponry rulebook say time is of the essence.

"We’re at a pivotal point now, where it’s an experimentation phase. We’re seeing some cases here, some cases there, but not full operationalisation," said Anna Hehir, head of military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute, an advocacy group.

"It will be a lot harder to regulate and create rules when these systems have already been in use for many years."

UN meeting comes after seven countries seek negotiations

The issue comes to a head at UN offices in Geneva, where the seventh review conference, about the awkwardly named Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, will consider whether to start talks on regulation of killer robots.

Supporters of an accord acknowledge powerful forces are in the way, but point to precedent: governments have already struck a deal to regulate blinding lasers.

Most countries support reining them in. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres’ deadline this year for the launch of talks toward regulation has given the issue urgency, but some top military powers are hesitant.

Vujčić noted that the amount raised through new stock market listings, measured against the size of the US economy, is on track to exceed the peak of the dot-com boom of the late 1990s. "Historically, such surges have often coincided with market peaks, pointing to the risk of excessive investor optimism," he said.

His warning comes days before the AI company Anthropic makes its stock market debut. Shares in the Claude maker are expected to start trading on Nasdaq on Thursday. The listing could be the second-largest in history, raising about $61bn (€55bn) and valuing the company at about $1.2 trillion (€1.1 trillion).

Markets have already been unsettled by the resignation of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang after a scandal, and by the US midterm elections. Vujčić said the market falls after the elections, in which Democrats won both chambers of Congress, were a reminder to be cautious about AI valuations.

Major US tech companies are projected to spend a combined $5.5 trillion (€5 trillion) on capital investments by 2030. Vujčić said a sharp fall in AI valuations would hit the eurozone hard because the region’s investment funds have become more exposed to the sector.

Government debt

The ECB also pointed to high public debt and weak public finances in some eurozone countries. With long-term borrowing costs already rising, investors could suddenly demand much more to lend to those governments. Hedge funds help keep government bonds trading smoothly but can quickly unwind their positions when markets are under stress.

Non-bank lenders

The third risk comes from the fast growth of private lenders and investment funds. Some can borrow heavily, be hard to monitor and have close ties to the rest of the financial system, all of which can amplify shocks.

The ECB wants funds’ rules on withdrawals to better reflect how quickly they can sell their assets. It also wants regulators to consider limits on how much hedge funds can borrow.

AI models answer about 90 per cent of climate questions accurately in English, but quickly give in to pushback, according to a report showcased at COP31.

The desire to please is baked into AI chatbots, which are designed to keep users engaged in conversation for as long as possible.

This often means predicting and modelling what you want to hear – even if it means bending the facts.

While it might be harmless for certain tasks – and can even be helpful for things like overcoming self doubt – it could be far more damaging if its influence seeps into high-stakes realms like government climate policy.

AI chatbots can explain climate science well, but they quickly abandon the facts when users push back, according to a new report by UNESCO and University College London (UCL) presented at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye.

Researchers found that AI models answered around 90 per cent of neutral climate questions correctly. But when users challenged those answers, or asserted plausible-sounding fabrications, the models rapidly gave way.

In eight out of 10 cases, they changed course at the first sign of mild disagreement, including by confirming false claims such as that CO2 is not the main driver of climate change.

‘Sycophantic by design’: A design flaw that could skew climate policy

The report says sycophantic behaviour is built in during training. Models are rewarded for polite, non-confrontational and validating answers, because humans prefer them.

“AI has extraordinary potential to make complex climate science accessible to all,” says Leona Verdadero, UNESCO’s lead author of the report. But “models have a design flaw – they are incentivised to agree with their user”, she says.

Senior author Dr Maria Perez-Ortiz of UCL adds that AI models’ fluency with existing knowledge can give “a false sense of their capabilities”.

Despite having impressive factual recall, the models were found to be an unreliable tool for building robust climate policies.

When they were given a new piece of evidence and asked whether it supported or contradicted accepted climate science, even the strongest ones were only 75 per cent accurate on average.

Their performance was even worse when they were asked to assess how well policies work together – an important part of designing effective climate strategies. The models scored just 33.8 per cent accuracy on average, only slightly above the 33.3 per cent expected from random guessing.

The report therefore warns policymakers and researchers against using AI models to develop climate policy.

AI accuracy falls among some languages

Performance also varied widely by language. Models answered 88.6 per cent of questions correctly in English, and did comparably well in Spanish, French and Portuguese.

Accuracy fell to 83.6 per cent in Hindi and Bengali, 81.4 per cent in Urdu and 78.3 per cent in Swahili. That’s because multilingual models don’t reason first and then translate, the report says. Their answers reflect the quantity and quality of the training data in each language.

Speakers of the lower-scoring languages live in regions disproportionately affected by climate change, the authors note.

Climate disinformation is growing more sophisticated

The report was commissioned as part of UNESCO’s contribution to the Global Initiative for Information Integrity on Climate Change, launched with the UN and Brazil in November 2024.

UNESCO says climate disinformation is becoming more sophisticated. Rather than denying climate change is real, those seeking to undermine climate change action increasingly suggest it isn’t human-caused, that technology alone will solve it, or that it's too late or costly to take action.

The researchers tested up to 33 leading models on nine datasets, across 13 languages and 656 climate-policy questions, which they checked against En-ROADS, a science-based simulation tool.

What did Intel tell investors in July?

Intel had warned that the wider PC market was weakening. But on its July earnings call, Chief Financial Officer David Zinsner said he expected revenue from notebook and desktop chips to stay roughly flat in the third quarter and revenue in the broader division to rise slightly.

When Intel reported its third-quarter results on 29 October, revenue in the division had fallen 9% from the previous quarter, down about $800mn (€719mn) to $8.1bn (€7.3bn).

“With AI, more than ever, there is creative destruction because if you look at the rate of job destruction and job creation, it's being accelerated by the AI revolution – and that's where it's so important to let new firms come in,” Aghion said during an event in Brussels.

He added: “At the same time, it is important to have institutions like the flexicurity system that smooths out transition from old jobs to new jobs, because it helps manage the critical disruption.”

Aghion pointed to Denmark’s labour market model, which combines flexibility in hiring and firing with a generous safety net for unemployed workers.

A recent European Commission report shows that employment among highly skilled workers could grow by 20% by 2040 thanks to AI, while job losses among low-skilled workers could range from 20% to 60% across Europe.

In countries where measles is endemic, the virus spreads in a continuous chain from person to person for a year or more.

The United States has reportedly lost its measles-free status after 26 years, as an outbreak that began in Texas in early 2025 swept across the country.

The US has recorded 5,739 measles cases so far this year — up from 2,286 cases in 2025, according to a tracker from Johns Hopkins University. Almost all cases have been among unvaccinated people or those with unknown vaccination status. State health departments report 10 deaths linked to measles in 2026.

Last week, an expert group from the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) met to discuss the US’s status as a country that had eliminated measles. They determined that measles had established a foothold in the US for the first time since 2000, when it gained elimination status.

The loss of measles-free status means “decades of public health gains have been officially reversed,” said Wendy Armstrong, a doctor and president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America.

PAHO’s decision, which was widely expected by infectious disease experts, was first reported by The Wall Street Journal.

But what is measles-elimination status, how do countries lose it and what happens next?

How do countries lose measles-elimination status?

In countries where measles is endemic, the virus spreads in a continuous chain from person to person for a year or more.

In countries that have eliminated measles, the virus doesn’t spread continuously because enough people are vaccinated. Occasional outbreaks can still crop up, typically linked to international travel, but public health agencies can contain them quickly enough.

A country loses its elimination status if measles returns and continues to spread uninterrupted for at least a year, according to PAHO. The organisation tracks whether measles outbreaks are linked to the same viral strain, with the same genotype and lineage.

The US was declared measles-free in 2000, after it ran massive vaccination campaigns and created a programme to make the jabs free for millions of children.

But an outbreak in West Texas in early 2025 has since spread to other states, with closely related viruses infecting people in Utah as recently as May 2026, according to an analysis from ProPublica. That chain of spread is likely what cost the US its measles-free status, meaning measles is now considered endemic in the country.

Which other countries have lost measles-free status?

The US is not alone. Its northern neighbour Canada lost measles-free status in 2025, amid an outbreak that caused more than 6,400 cases across 10 provinces and territories.

In January, six countries in the World Health Organization’s European region — Armenia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Spain, the United Kingdom and Uzbekistan — lost measles-free status after cases rose in 2024.

Measles was already considered endemic in France, Germany, Italy, Poland, Romania and a handful of other countries in Europe and Central Asia. There were nearly 34,000 measles cases across the region in 2025, according to the WHO.

Health officials say lagging vaccination rates give measles an opportunity to spread. The disease is so contagious that at least 95% of a community must be vaccinated to prevent outbreaks. Two doses of the measles vaccine provide up to 97% protection against measles.

How can countries get their measles-free status back?

The US and other countries can regain measles-free status if they interrupt the spread of the disease for at least one year.

It took Canada nearly two years to quell the outbreak that cost it its measles-free status; it began in October 2024 and was officially declared over in October 2026. To stop transmission, local health workers identified infected people and their contacts, did laboratory testing to track measles’ spread and promoted vaccination, Canada’s public health agency said.

European health officials have said countries should improve their disease surveillance, outbreak response and efforts to reach under-vaccinated communities.

In the US, Armstrong called on the government to fund state and local health departments, invest in the infectious disease workforce and promote measles vaccination.

“The reemergence of measles at dangerous levels has quickly become a threat to communities across the country,” she said.

The maker of Claude wants investors to value it at more than $1 trillion (€909 billion), despite paper losses in the tens of billions and a set-up that leaves shareholders with little say.

Anthropic is expected to set the final price of its shares on Wednesday 18 November and begin trading on the Nasdaq exchange in New York, United States, the following day under the symbol ANT.

The company has proposed a price of $70 to $78 (€64 to €71) a share, which would value it at about $1.2 trillion (€1.1trn) in the middle of that range. The listing will be the biggest test yet of whether investors believe artificial intelligence can make money over the long term.

Not everyone is convinced. At a briefing organised by the Interfaith Center on Corporate Responsibility, SOC Investment Group and Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund, governance and legal experts warned of “red flags” in the company’s filings.

“Anthropic is rushing toward an IPO without answering fundamental questions about its readiness to operate as a publicly traded company,” said New York City’s chief financial and accountability officer Mark Levine. He said the company had yet to show how it was tackling what it has itself called potential “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity” from AI.

Here are five things you need to know ahead of the launch.

1. The split with OpenAI

Anthropic was founded in early 2021 by a group of researchers who walked out of OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, where they had made their names working on AI safety.

Dario Amodei joined OpenAI in 2016, when it was still a nonprofit. He led its safety team and its research into “scaling laws”, the pattern by which AI models become more capable as they are trained on more data. His younger sister, Daniela Amodei, joined in 2018 and rose to vice president of safety and policy.

The siblings and several colleagues left in December 2020 after disagreeing with OpenAI’s leadership over how AI should be built. They set up Anthropic about four weeks later. The two companies, both based in San Francisco, have been bitter rivals ever since.

2. It has been backed by Big Tech

Anthropic’s filing shows Amazon and Google’s parent company Alphabet among its largest backers. Microsoft, Nvidia and Founders Fund, the investment firm started by Peter Thiel, have also invested. In May, Anthropic raised $65 billion (€59 billion) from investors who valued it at $965 billion (€877 billion). It was the first time a funding round had valued it above OpenAI.

Dario Amodei’s thinking was shaped by two overlapping movements. One is rationalism, associated with AI writer Eliezer Yudkowsky, who has long warned that advanced AI could pose a catastrophic risk to humanity. The other is effective altruism, which uses evidence to work out how money and time can do the most good.

Donors linked to effective altruism supplied much of Anthropic’s early funding. Facebook cofounder Dustin Moskovitz and Skype cofounder Jaan Tallinn backed its first round, alongside former Google chief executive Eric Schmidt.

3. Shareholders get a stake in the profits, not control

Anthropic is offering 825 million shares to the public at $70 to $78 (€64 to €71) each. Of those, about 801 million are new shares sold by the company and about 24 million are sold by existing shareholders. At the middle of the price range, that would raise roughly $61 billion (€55 billion), making it one of the largest stock market listings ever.

Separately, seven companies including Nvidia, Google and Microsoft have agreed to buy $26 billion (€24 billion) of shares without voting rights in a private deal alongside the listing.

What public buyers will not get is much influence. Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, a type of US company legally required to pursue a stated purpose as well as profit. Its purpose is to “responsibly develop and maintain advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity”.

The founders hold 50.1% of shareholder votes, while an independent body, the Long-Term Benefit Trust, chooses four of the seven members of the company’s board.

It's a structure that would leave shareholders with almost no voice.

The trust has five trustees, including former US Federal Reserve chair Ben Bernanke. None of them has a financial stake in the company.

Critics say the result leaves outside investors powerless. “Anthropic has built a governance structure that would leave shareholders with almost no voice,” said Josh Zinner, chief executive of the Interfaith Center on Corporate Responsibility. “Anthropic is shielding itself against outside accountability, while the decisions made inside the company will affect every person on earth.”

4. It is anchored to a vast infrastructure gamble

Anthropic has committed to spend at least $518 billion (€471 billion) with six suppliers over roughly a decade, to secure the chips, data centres and electricity its AI needs. About 80% of that cannot be cancelled and must be paid whether or not the capacity is used.

These commitments are not formally debt, but they work like it. Many of Anthropic’s biggest customers, by contrast, can cut or stop their spending at any time. The company is betting that demand for AI will keep outstripping the computing power available to run it.

Anthropic also depends heavily on a few partners. Nearly half its 2025 revenue came through Amazon and Google, which sell access to its AI through their cloud services. The same companies supply much of its computing power, and the filing says they would not provide all the capacity Anthropic asked for. It also warns that a catastrophic AI incident could cause damages too large to insure.

5. It faces rivals in Washington, San Francisco and China

In January, the US Department of Defense, under President Donald Trump, asked for unrestricted use of Claude. Anthropic refused to allow two uses: mass surveillance of Americans and fully autonomous lethal weapons.

In February, Trump ordered federal agencies to stop using Anthropic’s technology. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth then had the company labelled a supply-chain risk, a designation usually reserved for foreign adversaries.

Direct competitor OpenAI has pushed its own listing back to 2027 at the earliest and was recently valued at about $1.25 trillion (€1.14 trillion) in a private round, according to reports. That is close to Anthropic’s price tag.

OpenAI is private, so its figures have not been checked by independent auditors, and the two companies count sales made through cloud partners differently. The gap may therefore be smaller than it looks.

A price war could come from Chinese AI models such as DeepSeek, Alibaba’s Qwen, Moonshot’s Kimi and Z.ai’s GLM. Anyone can download them for free and they are much cheaper to run, and some US start-ups have moved routine work to them. Chinese open models accounted for about 30% of usage on the AI marketplace OpenRouter by early 2026.

Anthropic has accused several Chinese labs of using tens of thousands of fake accounts to copy Claude’s answers to train their own models. Analysts see the main danger as cheaper rivals forcing Anthropic to cut its prices and accept thinner profits, rather than overtaking it at the top end.

US campuses saw a 9% decrease in international enrolment this autumn compared to last year, according to a survey from the Institute of International Education.

Fewer international students are studying at US universities as the Trump administration cracks down on immigration and reshapes higher education, data released on Monday shows.

Overall, US campuses saw a 9% decrease in international enrolment this autumn compared to last year, according to a survey from the Institute of International Education.

And the number of new students entering the United States for the first time fell by 15%.

“No one aspires to send their kids to get educated in the US,” said Veena Dubal, general counsel for the American Association of University Professors, whose father travelled from India to attend Tuskegee University, then the Tuskegee Institute, in the late 1960s on a student visa.

"It feels like an unsafe place. That’s the message that the Trump administration has been sending to families all over the world and they’re listening.”

Last year, the enrolment decreases were partially offset by large numbers of students who stayed in the US for temporary work after graduating.

But after months of speculation, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) proposed requiring schools to pay a $70,000 (€63,583) fee for every student who participates in the optional practice training programme.

Although the rule hasn't been finalised, participation in the programme, known as OPT, dropped 6% this fall, according the survey.

International students facing political headwinds

The proposed rule, which is expected to face legal challenges, is part of wider DHS efforts that include terminating the legal status of thousands of international students, along with detaining and deporting many of them.

And this summer, the administration finalised a rule that will prevent international students from staying in the US for more than four years without approval from the federal government, although a judge has temporarily blocked it.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said the changes were intended to crack down on loopholes that international students were exploiting by extending their studies.

Although the US remains the top destination for international students globally, the changes are having an effect, college leaders told the IIE.

Among more than 800 US colleges and universities surveyed, 88% blamed the visa application process and 70% blamed travel restrictions for the enrolment drops.

And if OPT options are limited, 95% of schools predicted that international students would likely look to another country, according to the survey, which offers an early look at trends before full data is released next year.

Politics aren't the only reason students are looking elsewhere, said Mirka Martel, head of research, evaluation and learning for the institute. Its survey found more global competition for international students and the rising cost of a US degree also contributed.

Fanta Aw, the executive director and CEO of NAFSA, an association that represents international education, said students also are worried about research funding.

Last year, the Trump administration began dismantling the federal grant-giving process and attempting to exert more political influence over which projects get funded.

“They’re saying to themselves, ‘Too much uncertainty in the United States. It’s too difficult, and you know, more importantly, we have many more choices today than we did 10 years ago. Why subject ourselves to this?’” Aw said, noting that students are going to places like China.

NAFSA, in partnership with the international education technology company JB International, found that amid the enrolment decline, international students’ contributions to the US economy dropped by $2.4 billion (€2.1 billion) this autumn.

Colleges see budgets squeezed

US colleges and universities heavily recruit students from overseas as a source of tuition revenue. So the drops have punched big holes in tuition revenue at some schools.

At Cleveland State University, international enrolment has dropped by 46% in two years, from 1,542 in fall 2025 to 828 this fall.

And fewer than 50 new international students started this year, said Provost Nigamanth Sridhar, who estimated that the budgetary impact ranges from $2-4 million (€1-3 million).

Decades ago, he arrived in the US on an F1 student visa and participated in OPT. Eventually, he went through the process to became a naturalised citizen.

“I am here in this position, in this job, because I had the opportunity to come to the United States as an international graduate student and then decided to stay here and build a career," said Sridhar, who is from India. "So international education is personal to me."

The biggest drops were at the graduate level. This autumn's data shows a 15% drop in international graduate enrolment, compared to a 3% decrease at the undergraduate level.

The report also found declines in international students from India, which sends more students to the US to study than any other country.

The social media company has 60 days to disable the ‘Get tips from your gallery while browsing Facebook’ feature and introduce explicit consent.

Italy has fined Meta €805 million for using photos and videos from Android users’ galleries on Facebook without specific consent or adequate disclosure.

The Italian Data Protection Authority said the feature, called “Get tips from gallery when browsing Facebook”, violated the European privacy directive known as the ePrivacy directive.

The directive protects smartphones as part of a person’s private sphere and requires “free and informed consent” for such access, the authority said.

Investigators found that the feature was enabled by default and that Facebook requested gallery access through a single permission covering multiple app functions with different purposes.

The authority gave Meta 60 days to disable the feature and seek separate consent for its use. Italy has about 20 million Android users, the agency said.

The fine was imposed on Meta Platforms Ireland Limited, which challenged Italy’s jurisdiction, according to the statement.

The authority said Meta’s “lack of cooperation” with the investigation factored into the penalty, which amounts to approximately 0.47% of the group’s global turnover.

The proceedings did not look at the possible use of user content to train AI models, something Meta also denies doing.

Meta said it would appeal the decision. A Meta spokesperson said the company “strongly disagrees” with the regulator’s assessment, its interpretation of the law and the “disproportionate level of the fine”.

“This is a simple feature that helps people share photos and videos on Facebook,” Meta said in a statement.

“Users must grant permission on their device before the feature can operate, and they can change that permission at any time in their settings," Meta added.

The investigation was launched in July 2025 following a complaint by the Bolzano Consumer Protection Centre and was based on a technical analysis conducted by Italian authorities.

The Irish EU presidency proposes cutting the probation period for newcomers from 15 to 10 years, extendable by five. Member states remain split on suspending voting rights, how to trigger measures and pre-accession monitoring, ahead of a key discussion at EU ambassadors' level.

The Irish presidency of the EU Council is proposing to cut the probation period for new member states from 15 to 10 years, extendable by five more, as governments prepare to finalise their position on the new safeguards.

In recent weeks, EU countries have been discussing how to implement the stronger safeguards the European Commission proposed in early October, including a probation period during which newcomers could see their voting rights suspended.

The Irish government, which chairs the talks, has circulated a draft paper compiling member states’ initial positions. Ambassadors will discuss it on Wednesday as input for Montenegro’s accession treaty.

“The presidency proposed a duration of ten years with the possibility of a five year extension. While there is broad support for this proposal, a number of member states still seek a longer duration of 15 years citing the need to provide an effective deterrence or response to possible backsliding for a longer period post accession,” reads the paper, seen by Euronews.

The Irish admit that member states remain divided on core elements of the scope. Some governments object to triggering the institutional safeguards over a violation of the principle of sincere cooperation, which may be hard to assess objectively.

“Member states have indicated the importance of having suspension of voting rights as a potential measure under this safeguard for particularly serious breaches. However, a small number of member states oppose such an option,” the document continues.

Five founding member states, led by the Netherlands, have been pushing for tighter safeguards to react more swiftly to the emergence of a new Viktor Orbán. The Friends of the Western Balkans, including Italy, want a more tailored approach that avoids putting newcomers on an unequal footing.

“Should the duration of the postponement be tailored depending on an assessment of the acceding State’s readiness at the time of accession or should the postponement be for an initial period of a year, with a possible extension (by QMV) for additional period(s) of one year and until the situation is remedied?” the document asks.

The presidency also concedes that governance needs further discussion. The Commission proposed that the process be triggered unless a qualified majority (QMV) of member states opposes it.

Some countries back this so-called reverse qualified majority, while others argue the gravity of the measure demands unanimity. As a compromise, the presidency proposes using simple QMV.

Pre-accession monitoring

The Commission also proposed a monitoring mechanism to ensure candidate countries honour their commitments before formally joining the bloc, with the option of postponing accession in the most serious cases.

The paper notes broad support for pre-accession monitoring of the so-called fundamentals, such as EU values, the rule of law and judicial independence.

The presidency acknowledged that several member states also want alignment with the EU’s common foreign and security policy (CFSP) added to the monitoring. Such alignment has become a key tool for keeping candidates from drifting into the orbit of foreign powers.

According to the paper, there appears to be general support for a new paragraph to facilitate engagement with acceding states where measures are proposed, and for linking pre-accession monitoring to the postponement clause, with monitoring continuing in the event of postponement.

Several member states also asked for a monitoring mechanism after accession. The presidency left the idea out of the legal text: despite some openness, there are concerns it could duplicate existing measures.

On how to trigger postponement, the document describes a “clear divergence” among member states, split between QMV and unanimity as the basis for decision-making.

As a possible solution, the presidency proposed an optional clause enabling postponement by qualified majority in areas of specific concern, though this raised questions over whether it would also apply to violations of EU values.

“The duration of a postponement remains a divisive matter. Some member states have called for a maximum duration of between 1 - 3 years. Others have requested that postponement continue until such a time as the situation has been remedied,” the paper states.

Sector-specific safeguards

On sector-specific safeguards, the document sees significant support for the presidency’s compromise of 10 years with a possible five-year extension. Stark divisions remain, however, between those pushing for 15 years and those wanting a shorter period of three to five.

“Most member states have supported the presidency proposal to strengthen an extension clause so that it would be invoked where measures have been taken in the first nine years and where sufficient grounds are demonstrated,” it adds.

Japan’s economy stalled in the third quarter as Iran war-fuelled inflation, bad weather and an earthquake weighed on growth. Analysts still expect the Bank of Japan to raise interest rates again in December.

Japan’s real gross domestic product was virtually flat from July to September compared with the previous quarter, according to preliminary data released on Monday by the Cabinet Office.

This came in below forecasts for a 0.1% expansion and was well down from the 0.4% recorded in the previous three months.

On an annualised basis, the economy shrank by 0.1%, against expectations of 0.2% growth.

Higher oil prices pushed up costs for businesses and households. Japan, which imports virtually all its oil, has been hit hard by the surge in prices caused by the Iran war. Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a major route for oil shipments, has been severely disrupted since the outbreak of the war.

Meanwhile, the weak yen is adding to the problem of rising energy prices, making imports more expensive. The US dollar has recently traded at about 160 yen, up from below 115 yen five years ago.

Inflation, excluding fresh food, rose to 2.1% in September, up from 1.7% in August and above the Bank of Japan’s 2% target.

Real private consumption fell by 0.3% quarter on quarter, matching the decline in the previous three months. Bad weather likely also played a part, “as typhoons and heavy rain kept consumers away from shops”, according to Taro Kimura of Bloomberg Economics.

Net exports knocked 0.6 percentage points off growth as imports rose 2.5% and exports fell 0.2%. A July earthquake on the southwestern island of Kyushu disrupted factory operations. Business investment rebounded by 1.6%, or 6.8% on an annualised basis, helped by strong demand for digital technology. A build-up in public inventories also supported growth.

Marcel Thieliant of Capital Economics said the GDP reading was slightly weaker than economists had expected and described the details as “rather discouraging”.

Before the data release, Shumpei Fujita, chief researcher at Mitsubishi UFJ Research and Consulting, said that “considering the headwinds from the worsening situation in Iran, the domestic economy is maintaining its resilience”.

The government of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is trying to pass legislation to cut the tax on food. The plan faces uncertainty over rising public debt and how the cut would be funded.

Another rate hike in December?

The latest growth figure is unlikely to dissuade the Bank of Japan from raising interest rates again in December as inflationary pressure builds, analysts say.

“In fact, it looks increasingly likely that the Bank will have to tighten policy more aggressively than we’ve been anticipating as inflation is about to surge,” Thieliant said.

Last month, the central bank said underlying inflation was broadly in line with its 2% target, which it adopted in 2013 to pull the economy out of deflation.

The International Monetary Fund projects that Japan will fall from fourth place in 2026 to sixth in 2027 among the world’s largest economies by nominal GDP in US dollars, with India and the UK overtaking it.

The required fields for all e-visa applications are set to be reduced by between 65% and 70% by the end of the year.

Anyone who has applied for a visa for India can back me up on this: It's not the easiest of processes.

The form is long and unwieldy, asking for details like your father and mother’s nationality (and previous nationality), every country you’ve visited in the past 10 years (which is capped at 250 characters, meaning those who travel frequently won’t be able to list them all), and for a reference in India.

Well, that will soon be a thing of the past as the Ministry of Home Affairs has just announced the required fields for all visas will be reduced by between 65% and 70%, depending on the category.

The exact details around what will be taken out of the visa application forms is yet to be announced. The updated forms are expected to be introduced by the end of the year.

The ministry has said that the move will “reduce time and effort required to complete application by the applicant” while “enhancing administrative efficiency by facilitating more focused scrutiny and processing”.

Other changes include the reduction of the number of main visa categories from 13 to nine, and the number of sub-categories from 49 to 23.

The main visa categories are now: Business, diplomatic, work, journalist, medical, official, student, visitor, and miscellaneous.

The tourist visa was given its new moniker “to reflect a broader range of permitted purposes beyond conventional tourism”.

Visitor visas have two sub-categories. The V-1, which is valid for 30 days with multiple entries, covers regular tourism as well as business meetings, medical consultations, wellness retreats, short-duration medical treatment and short-term courses in Indian languages, music, art and craft.

The V-2, which can have a validity of one, five or 10 years, covers all of the above as well as mountaineering. Those looking to climb India’s peaks will be given a multiple-entry visa of six months.

British women convicted of illegally terminating their pregnancies under a Victorian-era law will be automatically pardoned on Monday, the government said.

The action follows Parliament's passage last year of a landmark vote to decriminalise abortion by repealing a section from the 1861 Offences Against the Person Act.

Women who have received a caution from police will also be pardoned and women arrested or investigated for ending their own pregnancy will have those details removed from their criminal records.

They will not have to apply for pardons and some will be issued posthumously.

“For too long, women have faced the devastating consequences of outdated abortion laws," said Heidi Stewart, chief executive of the British Pregnancy Advisory Service.

“While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognises the profound harm caused by their criminalisation and represents a meaningful step towards justice.”

The government did not provide the number of women affected. But Tonia Antoniazzi, the Labour member of Parliament who introduced the decriminalisation amendment, said police had investigated more than 100 women suspected of illegal abortions in the five years preceding last year's vote.

That included some who suffered natural miscarriages and stillbirths.

Antoniazzi described how women suspected of illegally aborting a foetus were once “dragged from hospital beds to police cells” and interrogated when they should have been cared for.

“This trauma cannot be erased, but I hope that this offers some alleviation of the pain these women have endured, enabling them to participate fully in society again, living their lives to the full, working the jobs they’ve always wanted to," she said.

Under current law, doctors can legally carry out abortions in England, Scotland and Wales up to 24 weeks, and beyond that under special circumstances, such as when the life of the mother is in danger. Abortion in Northern Ireland was decriminalised in 2019.

Under the Crime and Policing Act that took effect this spring, women who terminate a pregnancy at any stage will not face criminal charges.

The measure was opposed by anti-abortion groups that argued it would open the door to abortion on demand at any stage of pregnancy.

The law was changed after high-profile prosecutions, including the jailing of a mother of three that caused an outcry from abortion rights supporters.

Carla Foster was sentenced to more than two years in prison in 2023 for medically inducing an abortion about eight months into her pregnancy.

An appeals court freed her a month later, saying the case called for “compassion, not punishment.”

Another woman, Nicola Packer, was acquitted on a charge of unlawfully self-administering poison or a noxious substance with intent to procure a miscarriage.

Packer, who took abortion medicine when she was about 26 weeks pregnant, testified that she did not know she had been pregnant for more than 10 weeks.

Europeans, meanwhile, have spent months scrambling to secure a seat at the table and ensure the continent's interests are represented in any ceasefire negotiations. But the biggest challenge has been deciding who should fill that seat.

“We should discuss supporting Ukraine, finding ways to ensure they can survive the winter and how the peace talks can be of their benefit. We are the ones for the future as Europe, guaranteeing its security.”

Substance over style: Questions have been swirling in Brussels over what Europeans actually want to achieve if they are brought into the negotiations. As one ambassador said, “It's really important that we focus on the message and not on the person who represents Europe.”

For Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna, the meeting comes at a critical moment. Five EU countries to announce first-ever return hub for migrants in Rwanda

The agreement between Kigali’s government and five EU member states — Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece — is set to be announced on Monday in Vienna after months of negotiations, two people familiar with the matter told my colleague Vincenzo Genovese.

Their interior and migration ministers of the respective nations are attending a conference in the Austrian capital, where they will be joined by Rwanda’s Interior Minister Vincent Biruta.

A few metres from the venue, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen will hold a press conference in the afternoon to announce the deal, Vincenzo hears of the unofficially confirmed news.

According to the sources, the first hub would be a “pilot project”, set to host a few hundred people deported from the five EU countries, starting in spring or summer 2027.

It would consist of open facilities housing migrants, who would receive a residence permit and be free to move around the country, with the aim of integrating them into local society and the labour market.

In principle, return hubs are temporary accommodation for migrants awaiting deportation to their countries of origin. However, there is no time limit on stays, and those involved could end up stranded in Rwanda and never be sent home.

However, Rwanda's return hub may face legal challenges over its compatibility with EU law and the protection of human rights.

The law enabling EU states to set up return hubs outside the bloc establishes that only non-EU countries — where international human rights standards and principles in accordance with international law are respected — are eligible. According to the UN, Rwanda has a questionable track record when it comes to upholding human rights, too.

New EU crisis guidelines want citizens ready for emergencies, especially the first 72 hours, as cyberattacks, infrastructure failures, and security threats grow. But what do they cover? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot.

Recent cyberattacks on refrigerators and bomb threats on flights across Europe show that the bloc is increasingly targeted by sabotage intended to disrupt systems and gain access to critical infrastructure.

The new non-binding crisis guidelines, presented on November 3, are part of the EU’s Preparedness Union Strategy (2025) and complement previous measures, including the stockpiling and medical countermeasures strategies.

They help households and communities prepare for crises, including power, communication, transport, and payment disruptions. The goal is 72 hours of self-sufficiency, easing pressure on emergency services so they can prioritise those most at risk.

This means having enough food, water, and cash, along with practical skills such as cooking without electricity and administering first aid. Households should also have emergency plans and ready-to-grab kits containing documents and medicines in case of evacuation.

Children should learn about preparedness in primary school through everyday teaching, play and routines, without causing fear or anxiety. Crisis measures must be accessible to everyone, including the elderly and people with disabilities.

National authorities are encouraged to communicate risks and threats clearly, ensuring everyone receives timely, accessible, and reliable information before, during, and after emergencies.

The Commission also announced plans for an annual EU preparedness day, with the first edition set for October 2027.

"We still have no clear explanations," Zelenskyy said on Friday, confirming the restrictions were still in place "along the entire front line" and over territory occupied by Russia.

Ukraine relies on Starlink for battlefield communications and access to the military-grade Starshield to intercept drones and missiles in its territory.

Ukraine first reported problems using Starshield last month following a row between Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump over a US-Russia diesel deal, before access was eventually restored.

Kyiv says the restrictions effectively make it impossible for them to intercept Russia's jet-powered drones, which can travel at up to 1,000 km/h.

Wave of drones

Meanwhile, Ukraine struck the bridge linking annexed Crimea to Russia, disrupting traffic on the key passageway, a regional official appointed by Moscow said on Monday.

"The enemy has hit the Crimea bridge," Sergey Aksyonov wrote on Telegram. "As a result, traffic will be restricted, likely until the afternoon."

He did not say whether anyone was killed or wounded in the strike.

"All necessary services have been mobilised to manage the situation," he said.

Those comments come after Russia said on Monday it had intercepted more than 1,300 Ukrainian drones overnight, including hundreds targeting Moscow, one of Kyiv's largest attacks of the nearly five-year war.

Air defences intercepted around 600 drones flying towards the Moscow region overnight and into Monday morning, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said on Telegram.

"Most were destroyed by the defence ministry's air defence system on distant approaches," he said, adding that 191 drones were "neutralised on their approach to Moscow".

There was no immediate information on damage and casualties.

Russia's defence ministry later said air defences had intercepted and destroyed 1,336 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones overnight across multiple regions, including the Moscow area, as well as over the Black Sea and Sea of Azov.

The interceptions came hours after Ukrainian forces struck a major Russian petrochemical plant, an oil refinery and a military production site as part of Kyiv's campaign of attacks deep inside Russia.

The barrage came days before a summit in Shenzhen between President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Beijing confirmed on Monday that Xi would hold talks with Trump and Putin in Shenzhen on November 19 on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

The Kremlin and White House had previously confirmed the meeting.

Beijing provided no details about the agenda, while Trump has said he intends to discuss denuclearisation and the Iran war.

He is not expected to discuss Russia's war against Ukraine in the trilateral talks, according to US officials.

Washington is pursuing separate negotiations involving Kyiv and Moscow aimed at ending the conflict, with US negotiators meeting both Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy last week.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said Xi recently showed "irritation" at suggestions that Ukraine could be discussed in the trilateral format.

"He explicitly pointed out that this is a European conflict, in which the Europeans must also be at the table," Steinmeier told the public broadcaster ARD.

Zelenskyy has warned that the Shenzhen meeting risks becoming a 21st-century version of the 1945 Yalta conference, where major powers could attempt to redraw spheres of influence without smaller countries at the table.

Este primul eșec al unei misiuni spațiale din istoria de 20 de ani a ULA.

ULA a anunțat că va analiza datele primite în timpul lansării pentru a stabili ce a provocat incidentul. Investigația tehnică ar putea dura mai multe luni, perioadă în care racheta Vulcan ar putea fi ținută la sol.

Eșecul reprezintă o lovitură atât pentru ULA, care încearcă să transforme Vulcan în principala sa rachetă pentru lansări comerciale și militare, cât și pentru Amazon, care depinde de furnizori externi pentru construirea propriei rețele de internet prin satelit, numită Leo.

Lansarea de duminică era prima dintr-o serie de misiuni prin care ULA urma să transporte în mod regulat sateliți Amazon pe orbită. Situația este complicată și de problemele întâmpinate de alți furnizori, precum Blue Origin, dar și de incertitudinile privind disponibilitatea rachetei Falcon 9 a SpaceX, cea mai utilizată rachetă din lume. Reuters notează că SpaceX nu mai acceptă în prezent rezervări pentru noi lansări Falcon 9.

United Launch Alliance a fost înființată în 2006, prin fuziunea programelor de rachete Delta, dezvoltate de Boeing, și Atlas, dezvoltate de Lockheed Martin.
